correctness.rationale: For every \(0<q<1\) and integer \(n\ge1\), the proof reconstructs the Bloch matrix and its sharp singular-value lower bounds. At \(n=2\), intersecting transverse planes force a singular value \(q^2\); the determinant fixes the product of the other two, and arithmetic--geometric mean gives \(2q+q^2\), achieved by a quarter-turn. At \(n\ge3\), the determinant yields \(3q^{2n/3}\). The explicit feasible \(SO(3)\) rotation has eigenvalues \(q^{2/3}\) and \(q^{2/3}e^{\pm2\pi i/n}\), so its Bloch matrix has exact power \(q^{2n/3}I_3\) by distinct-root diagonalizability. The construction explicitly proves its feasibility inequalities. Every such rotation is implemented by a qubit unitary. The established unital-qubit entanglement-breaking criterion \(\|A^n\|_*\le1\) then gives sharp inclusive thresholds. The verification program completed 1673 numerical consistency assertions at finitely many parameters and depths; the general statement rests on the analytic proof.

value.rationale: The sharp finite-depth optimal entanglement-breaking control of repeated dephasing is a natural experimentally implementable design invariant. A time-homogeneous rotation realizes an exact isotropic depolarizing power at every prescribed depth \(n\ge3\), providing a surprising equality in a determinant/nuclear-norm bound; \(n=2\) instead has a structurally forced singular direction and a different threshold. These are a complete parameterized classification with realizable controls, not isolated data or a textbook restatement. The known unchanged-axis dephasing obstruction highlights the nontrivial role of rotation.
